claims.text: Retention of toughness in high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by the stability and distribution of nanoscale secondary precipitates.
Thermal aging can cause nanoscale secondary precipitates to coarsen.
Precipitate coarsening reduces the precipitates' ability to deflect cracks.
Precipitate coarsening reduces the precipitates' ability to accommodate plastic deformation.
Loss of crack deflection and plastic-deformation accommodation due to coarsening reduces toughness.
Rapid solidification can produce a fine, homogeneous dispersion of nanoscale secondary precipitates in a high-entropy alloy.
A fine, homogeneous dispersion of nanoscale secondary precipitates contributes to enhanced toughness.
A controlled thermal-aging treatment can induce precipitate growth without forming entirely new phases.
Isothermal aging at a sufficiently high temperature and increasing durations will capture the evolution of precipitate coarsening.
Precipitate size and spatial distribution are the structural mediators of toughness.
Fine, dispersed precipitates act as crack deflectors.
Fine, dispersed precipitates act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Crack deflection and impeded dislocation motion promote energy absorption during deformation.
Coarsened precipitates provide sites for stress concentration.
Aged samples with coarsened precipitates will exhibit lower toughness than the freshly prepared baseline with fine, uniformly dispersed precipitates.
The proposed relationship applies only when precipitate coarsening occurs without phase transformations or independent toughness-altering mechanisms such as grain-boundary embrittlement.
The aging temperature and duration needed to produce a coarse precipitate distribution vary among alloy compositions.
